They found a heterozygous gly2019-to-ser (G2019S) mutation in 4 of the 61 families (6.6%). The families came from Italy, Portugal, and Brazil, which showed that the mutation occurs in different populations.
quotes: identified a heterozygous mutation (Gly2019 ser) present in four of 61 (6.6%) unrelated families with Parkinson's disease and autosomal dominant inheritance
The families originated from Italy, Portugal, and Brazil, indicating the presence of the mutation in different populations.

findings.statement: Di Fonzo et al. (2005) reported that the phenotype associated with the LRRK2 G2019S mutation was broad and included both early and late disease onset.
quotes: The associated phenotype was broad, including early and late disease onset.

phenotypes.text: parkinsonism with early or late onset

findings.statement: Di Fonzo et al. (2005) concluded that LRRK2 G2019S is a common mutation associated with dominantly inherited Parkinson disease. It was present in 6.6% of the unrelated autosomal dominant families they studied.
quotes: identify a common mutation associated with dominantly inherited Parkinson's disease

relevance_reason: The paper reports how often the LRRK2 G2019S mutation occurs in familial Parkinson disease, which is the PARK8 subject.

findings.statement: Nichols et al. (2005) screened genomic DNA from 767 affected individuals in 358 multiplex families with familial Parkinson disease, plus controls, for the LRRK2 gly2019-to-ser (G2019S) mutation. Thirty-five affected individuals (5%) carried the mutation: 34 were heterozygous and 1 was homozygous. The authors suggested that this single LRRK2 mutation causes Parkinson disease in 5% of individuals with familial disease.
quotes: Of 767 affected individuals from 358 multiplex families, 35 (5%) individuals were either heterozygous (34) or homozygous (one) for the mutation
Thus, our results suggest that a single LRRK2 mutation causes Parkinson's disease in 5% of individuals with familial disease.

findings.statement: Nichols et al. (2005) reported that individuals carrying the LRRK2 G2019S mutation had clinical findings typical of idiopathic Parkinson disease.
quotes: and had typical clinical findings of idiopathic Parkinson's disease

findings.statement: Nichols et al. (2005) recommended that screening for the LRRK2 G2019S mutation be part of genetic testing for Parkinson disease.
quotes: Screening for this mutation should be a component of genetic testing for Parkinson's disease.

relevance_reason: Identifies LRRK2 mutations as the cause of PARK8 autosomal dominant parkinsonism and describes pleomorphic pathology.

findings.statement: Zimprich et al. (2004) used high-resolution recombination mapping and candidate gene sequencing in 46 families with autosomal dominant, late-onset parkinsonism previously linked to chromosome 12p11.2-q13.1 (PARK8) and found 6 disease-segregating mutations (5 missense and 1 putative splice site mutation) in the LRRK2 gene.
quotes: By high-resolution recombination mapping and candidate gene sequencing in 46 families, we have found six disease-segregating mutations (five missense and one putative splice site mutation) in a gene encoding a large, multifunctional protein, LRRK2 (leucine-rich repeat kinase 2).

findings.statement: Zimprich et al. (2004) noted that they had previously linked families with autosomal dominant, late-onset parkinsonism to chromosome 12p11.2-q13.1 (PARK8), and refined the region by high-resolution recombination mapping.
quotes: We have previously linked families with autosomal-dominant, late-onset parkinsonism to chromosome 12p11.2-q13.1 (PARK8).

findings.statement: Zimprich et al. (2004) reported 6 postmortem examinations of affected mutation carriers from families A and D that showed brainstem dopaminergic degeneration accompanied by strikingly diverse pathologies, including Lewy body Parkinson disease, diffuse Lewy body disease, nigral degeneration without distinctive histopathology, and progressive supranuclear palsy-like pathology. Clinical diagnoses of parkinsonism with dementia, amyotrophy, or both were also noted.
quotes: Within affected carriers of families A and D, six post mortem diagnoses reveal brainstem dopaminergic degeneration accompanied by strikingly diverse pathologies.

These include abnormalities consistent with Lewy body Parkinson's disease, diffuse Lewy body disease, nigral degeneration without distinctive histopathology, and progressive supranuclear palsy-like pathology.
Clinical diagnoses of Parkinsonism with dementia or amyotrophy or both, with their associated pathologies, are also noted.

findings.statement: Zimprich et al. (2004) noted that LRRK2 belongs to the ROCO protein family, containing a MAPKKK-class protein kinase domain and several other major functional domains, and suggested that LRRK2 may be central to the pathogenesis of several major neurodegenerative disorders associated with parkinsonism.
quotes: It belongs to the ROCO protein family and includes a protein kinase domain of the MAPKKK class and several other major functional domains.
Hence, LRRK2 may be central to the pathogenesis of several major neurodegenerative disorders associated with parkinsonism.

relevance_reason: The paper reports cloning the PARK8 gene (dardarin), which contains missense mutations that segregate with PARK8-linked Parkinson disease in families from England and Spain.

findings.statement: Paisán-Ruíz et al. (2004) cloned a novel gene in the PARK8 region and found missense mutations in it that segregated with PARK8-linked Parkinson disease in 5 families from England and Spain.
quotes: We describe here the cloning of a novel gene that contains missense mutations segregating with PARK8-linked PD in five families from England and Spain.

findings.statement: Paisán-Ruíz et al. (2004) named the protein encoded by the PARK8 gene 'dardarin', from the Basque word 'dardara', meaning tremor. They chose this name because of the tremor seen in Parkinson disease and because several of the families were of Basque descent.
quotes: Because of the tremor observed in PD and because a number of the families are of Basque descent, we have named this protein dardarin, derived from the Basque word dardara, meaning tremor.

findings.statement: Paisán-Ruíz et al. (2004) noted that PARK8, identified by Funayama and colleagues in 2002, appears to be a common cause of familial Parkinson disease.
quotes: PARK8, identified in 2002 by Funayama and colleagues, appears to be a common cause of familial PD.

relevance_reason: Clinical and neuropathologic follow-up of a kindred with autosomal dominant parkinsonism; the authors suggested linkage to the PARK8 locus on chromosome 12.

findings.statement: Wszolek et al. (2004) reported follow-up of a parkinsonian kindred first described in 1995. Since that report, 4 more individuals had become affected, with a mean age at onset of 65 years. All 4 had the cardinal signs of Parkinson disease and responded well to levodopa.
quotes: Since the original 1995 report of a parkinsonian kindred, four individuals have been affected (mean age at onset, 65 years).
All four had cardinal signs of Parkinson disease (PD) and good response to levodopa.

phenotypes.hpo_label: Parkinsonism with favorable response to dopaminergic medication

findings.statement: Wszolek et al. (2004) reported 4 autopsies in the kindred. All 4 showed neuronal loss and gliosis in the substantia nigra, but the other pathology varied. One case had Lewy bodies limited to brainstem nuclei and a second had diffuse Lewy bodies. A third had neurofibrillary tangles without Lewy bodies, and the fourth had neither neurofibrillary tangles nor Lewy bodies.
quotes: Four autopsies showed neuronal loss and gliosis in the substantia nigra.
Lewy bodies (LB) limited to brainstem nuclei were detected in one case, diffuse LB in the second, neurofibrillary tangles (NFT) without LB in the third, and neither NFT nor LB in the fourth.

phenotypes.text: neuronal loss and gliosis in the substantia nigra

findings.statement: In this autosomal dominant parkinsonism kindred, Wszolek et al. (2004) reported that genetic studies suggested linkage to the PARK8 locus on chromosome 12.
quotes: Genetic studies suggested linkage to the PARK8 locus on chromosome 12.

relevance_reason: Linkage study that confirms the PARK8 locus on chromosome 12 in white families with autosomal dominant parkinsonism and narrows the candidate interval.

findings.statement: Zimprich et al. (2004) tested 21 white families with Parkinson disease and a pattern compatible with autosomal dominant transmission (at least 3 affected individuals in more than 1 generation) for linkage to the PARK8 region on centromeric chromosome 12, using 29 markers. In total they tested 167 family members (84 affected, 83 unaffected). Assuming heterogeneity and using an affecteds-only model, they obtained a maximum multipoint lod score of 2.01 (P = 0.0047) in the whole sample, with an estimated 0.32 proportion of linked families.
quotes: We tested 21 white families with Parkinson disease and an inheritance pattern compatible with autosomal dominant transmission for linkage in this region.
One hundred sixty-seven family members were tested (84 affected and 83 unaffected).
a maximum multipoint LOD score of 2.01 was achieved in the total sample, with an estimated proportion of families with linkage of 0.32

findings.statement: Zimprich et al. (2004) found that 2 families, family A (German Canadian) and family D (from western Nebraska), each showed significant linkage to PARK8. Their combined maximum multipoint lod score was 3.33 under an affecteds-only model and 3.92 under a penetrance-dependent model. The 1-lod support interval placed the disease locus between a CA repeat on genomic clone AC025253 (44.5 Mb) and marker D12S1701 (47.7 Mb).
quotes: Two families (family A [German Canadian] and family D [from western Nebraska]) reached significant linkage on their own, with a combined maximum multipoint LOD score of 3.33, calculated with an affecteds-only model
When a penetrance-dependent model was calculated, the combined multipoint LOD score achieved was 3.92 (family A: LOD score 1.68, P=.0027; family D: LOD score 2.24, P=.0007).
the most likely disease location is between a CA repeat polymorphism on genomic clone AC025253 (44.5 Mb) and marker D12S1701 (47.7 Mb)

findings.statement: Zimprich et al. (2004) concluded that the PARK8 locus causes disease in a subset of white families with autosomal dominant parkinsonism, with an estimated 0.32 proportion of linked families. They suggested that PARK8 could be a more common locus.
quotes: Our data provide evidence that the PARK8 locus is responsible for the disease in a subset of families of white ancestry with autosomal dominant parkinsonism, suggesting that it could be a more common locus.

relevance_reason: This is the original paper that mapped the PARK8 locus in a Japanese family with autosomal dominant parkinsonism and gave the locus its name.

findings.statement: Funayama et al. (2002) performed genomewide linkage analysis in a Japanese family with autosomal dominant parkinsonism. Parametric two-point analysis gave a maximum lod score of 4.32 at D12S345 (12p11.21), and multipoint analysis gave a maximum lod score of 4.71 at D12S85 (12q12). Haplotype analysis found obligate recombinations at D12S1631 and D12S339, which defined a 13.6-cM disease-associated interval in 12p11.2-q13.1. Nonparametric two-point and multipoint analyses gave maximum lod scores of 14.2 and 24.9 at D12S345.
quotes: Parametric two-point linkage analysis yielded a highest log odds (LOD) score of 4.32 at D12S345 (12p11.21). Parametric multipoint linkage analysis of the 13.6cM interval around this marker yielded LOD scores almost uniformly of >4.0 with a Z(max) of 4.71 at D12S85 (12q12).
Haplotype analysis detected two obligate recombination events at D12S1631 and D12S339 and defined the disease-associated haplotype in the 13.6cM interval in 12p11.2-q13.1.

Nonparametric two-point and multipoint linkage analyses, which are penetrance-independent, yielded Z(max) LOD scores of 14.2 and 24.9 at D12S345, respectively, strongly supporting the mapping of the parkinsonism locus in this family to 12p11.23-q13.11.

findings.statement: Funayama et al. (2002) described a Japanese family with autosomal dominant parkinsonism whose clinical features were compatible with those of common Parkinson disease.
quotes: We performed genomewide linkage analysis of a Japanese family with autosomal dominant parkinsonism, which exhibits clinical features compatible with those of common Parkinson's disease.

findings.statement: Funayama et al. (2002) found that all patients in the family shared the disease-associated haplotype, but some unaffected individuals also carried it. They suggested that penetrance in this family was incomplete and that environmental or other genetic factors modify expression of the disease.
quotes: This haplotype was shared by all the patients and by some unaffected carriers, suggesting that disease penetration in this family is incomplete.
This low penetrance suggests that environmental or other genetic factors modify expression of the disease.

findings.statement: Funayama et al. (2002) noted that this chromosome 12 region differs from every known locus for hereditary parkinsonism.
quotes: This chromosome region is different from any known locus for hereditary parkinsonism, in keeping with the unique genetic features of the parkinsonism in this family.

findings.statement: Funayama et al. (2002) named the new parkinsonism locus on chromosome 12p11.2-q13.1 PARK8.
quotes: The nomenclature of PARK8 was assigned to the new locus.

relevance_reason: Describes the Sagamihara family, a large Japanese family with autosomal dominant Parkinson disease and no Lewy bodies, relevant to PARK8.

findings.statement: Hasegawa and Kowa (1997) reported a family from Sagamihara City (Japan) with Parkinson disease across 5 generations. The clinical features did not differ from those of common Parkinson disease, and the title notes older age at onset and a good response to levodopa therapy.
quotes: Autosomal dominant Parkinson's disease in 5 generations of a family living in Sagamihara City is reported.
Clinical features of this family did not differ from common PD
older onset of age, and good response to levodopa therapy

phenotypes.hpo_label: Parkinsonism with favorable response to dopaminergic medication

findings.statement: Hasegawa and Kowa (1997) reported that Parkinson disease was inherited in an autosomal dominant pattern through 5 generations of the Sagamihara family.
quotes: Autosomal dominant Parkinson's disease in 5 generations of a family living in Sagamihara City is reported.

findings.statement: In autopsied members of the Sagamihara family, Hasegawa and Kowa (1997) found neuropathology that differed from typical Parkinson disease. Loss of melanin-containing cells was mild to moderate, and the number of locus ceruleus neurons was maintained. No Lewy bodies were found in any region where Lewy bodies frequently appear in Parkinson disease.
quotes: In autopsied cases, the loss of melanin-containing cells was mild to moderate, and the number of neurons of the locus ceruleus was maintained.
No Lewy bodies were detected at all from any region where Lewy bodies frequently appear in PD.

phenotypes.text: mild to moderate loss of melanin-containing neurons

phenotypes.hpo_label: Neuronal loss in central nervous system

relevance_reason: The abstract describes cloning a cDNA for DP-1, a DNA-binding component of the transcription factor DRTF1/E2F. It does not mention Parkinson disease, LRRK2, the PARK8 locus or any patients, so a curator would not cite it in the PARK8 entry.
Describes family D, a large Western Nebraska kindred with autosomal dominant parkinsonism resembling idiopathic PD; clinical, PET and autopsy findings for this phenotype.

findings.statement: Wszolek et al. (1995) described a large family (family D) from western Nebraska, whose ancestors probably immigrated to the United States from England, with 188 individuals spanning 6 generations and 18 affected members. Affected members developed typical levodopa-responsive Parkinson disease with bradykinesia, rigidity, resting tremor, and impaired postural reflexes; eye movement abnormalities, pyramidal and cerebellar signs, sensory disturbances, and orthostatic blood pressure changes did not occur. Disease progression was slow.
quotes: We studied a family (family D) whose ancestors probably immigrated to the United States from England. The pedigree contains 188 individuals spanning six generations with 18 affected members.

Typical levodopa-responsive PD with bradykinesia, rigidity, resting tremor, and impaired postural reflexes develops. Eye movement abnormalities, pyramidal and cerebellar signs, sensory disturbances, and orthostatic blood pressure changes do not occur. Disease progression is slow.

phenotypes.hpo_label: Parkinsonism with favorable response to dopaminergic medication

findings.statement: Wszolek et al. (1995) found that parkinsonism in family D was inherited in an autosomal dominant pattern.

findings.statement: Wszolek et al. (1995) reported that PET with [18F]-6-fluoro-L-dopa in an affected member of family D showed decreased fluorodopa uptake in a pattern consistent with Parkinson disease, and autopsy of another affected member showed neuronal and pigmentary loss, gliosis, and Lewy bodies in the substantia nigra pars compacta. The authors concluded that the disorder closely resembled, if not identical to, idiopathic PD.
quotes: PET with [18F]-6-fluoro-L-dopa (FD) performed on an affected individual revealed decreased uptake of FD in a pattern consistent with PD.
Autopsy performed on another affected individual demonstrated neuronal and pigmentary loss, gliosis, and Lewy bodies in the substantia nigra pars compacta.
This large kindred appears to represent a neurodegenerative disorder closely resembling, if not identical to, idiopathic PD.
